The course of disease

The refugees from Niar described the grey sea in this way. At first, a man gets chills, but by the fire passes. On the second day, fatigue piles up: work does not go, sweat pours from a bucket of water. On the third blue lips - "blue kiss", after which it is better to stay away from the patient. Then the fingers and nose turn blue, there are gray circles under the eyes, the skin turns pale, the patient is chilled - then he is no longer a resident. On the fifth or sixth day, suffocation begins, the patient grabs air with his mouth like a fish, and dies in the morning. Louise explained the name as follows: “the sick muzzles are blue and the lips swell.” (Louisa) According to Ethan, death from the sea is slow, the patient can suffer for weeks; therefore, a sudden “death from the sea” overnight causes suspicion of poison. In the first days, the disease is not visible, and an apparently healthy person can carry the infection.

As the sea is transmitted, no one knows for sure: the scientist physician admits that there is no consensus on the sea diseases - the gray sea, the garlands, the ulcers. The refugees were afraid to even speak to the sick. More does not understand classes: refugees from Niar were listed among the dead and cooks, and knights, and burgomaster, and all remembered beauty - the daughter of the bishop. The painter claimed that even a dog had died from the sea, “lying in a pond all blue.” The old woman May objected that it was a drowned shoemaker's dog, blue from the breed, and she was struck off the victim list. According to the old soldier Doxet, in the army of the one who began to turn blue, they put him in a deaf van and kept him there “until he dies or gets sick”, and could also set fire. (Doxett)

Treatment

There is no reliable means in the “underworld”. The people are treated for what they are doing: with silver (agate in wine - so advised the "scientist", who wore a bird's beak and mask), reading sixteen prayers to the Foremothers and ninety-six to the Forefathers, an ice bath or, conversely, a steam room. Harmon listed other medicinal products - rat legs, a widow's web - and believed that they were all "like a horse crutches." He warned David not to go to Niar, but he reminded him that he had also destroyed many of the noblest seas. Only Sacred Objects are able to heal the sea, and the healing of the sea is considered an obvious miracle of the Subject. Robert Origin told Erwin the story of the Flower of Life of Susan Pramati: each of his sixteen petals could cure any disease once. One day, a tiny girl was brought to Susan, sick with a gray pestilence, “and this is a contagious disease.” The girl should be immediately healed or locked in prison, so as not to infect the whole city. Susan tore one of the eight remaining petals, and an hour later the girl was healthy. The girl was the daughter of Susan herself, but the Mother still said: “Sorry.” Father David acknowledged that in the sublunar world there is no means, and the Objects are “silent.” He dreamed that someday people will learn to talk with objects and stop the sea.

Epidemic of 1774

In the spring of 1774, the sea broke out in Niar. By April 12, when Harmon came to the Lighthouse, he was already walking “half the moon.” The refugees were arguing about its cause. Some claimed that the sea brought a dozen free riders-Westerners who jumped a month before either from Halliwell or Reis: the first to fall ill was a laundress from Honey Street, whose stepdaughter “got mixed up with the horses”, and the riders themselves jumped healthy. The very same stepdaughter, to everyone's surprise, remained "alive and healthy." The old painter objected that the gods sent the disease, because people “do not live according to the commandments.” The townspeople fled in all directions; Harmon picked up eight refugees in the Clue. Among them was Polly's young widow: her husband, woodcarver John, had died two weeks earlier. Imperial troops cordoned off the city, and Adrian refused to release even the healthy. Food and water were delivered to Niar, all work, except medical and sanitary, was canceled. The townspeople were told not to leave their homes, not to communicate with each other and not to attend temples and meetings, and worship services and funeral processions were forbidden. Father David went to Niar to console the dying: “People need to believe and hope.” He survived: “More couldn’t handle me. I’m sorry, just like I am with him.”

The fear of the sea almost cost the life of a child in the circle of Harmon. When the grandson of the painter, Malyarenko, trembled with chills under a cold shower, the companions demanded to expel him into the field. Louise offered to "throw the hell out" of the boy, Snip - and grandfather at the same time. Harmon hesitated. Polly argued that the mor does not grow so quickly: "I saw how they die from the blue sea." She stood next to the boy, and Snape said that now we must expel her. Joaquin stopped the dispute: he drove the sword into the floor of the van and told everyone to go to bed. In the morning, Malyarenko, "as it suits a cold," coughed and sneezed, and "nothing like a gray sea" was in it.

The petitioners, who had relatives in Niar, in an open audience asked Adrian to release from the cordon at least healthy relatives examined by doctors. Mira, watching this, understood the difficulty of choice: in the first days, the mor is invisible, and an apparently healthy person can carry the infection.

According to David’s father, two thousand and three hundred people in Niar, five hundred in the surrounding villages, and four hundred in Izluchina carried away the sea. By the summer the epidemic stopped: in early July 1774, the owner of the hotel complained that the sea was over and people had run out.

Aftermath

Niar was depopulated, and the rate of tax dues assigned from all over the city and each shop remained the same. In February 1775, when Iona and Mark passed through the Niar, the townspeople complained that the tax collectors had emptied them to the thread and a double load was laid on each burgher. In the spring of 1775, “bleeded by last year’s sea,” Niar, like Lowville, supported Salem’s rebels.

Other cases

  • The baron of Smolensk died of the sea in 1772 ("in the year before last", according to Harmon): in the coffin he lay with blue lips and "purple face, as if in blue juice".
  • Baron Rosbet of the South Road, one of the heirs to the throne, died in the spring of 1774 "from the blue sea." According to his death certificate, he turned blue face, suffocated, let foam from his mouth and died the same night. Ethan noticed that sissy death is slow, and in one night it does not kill. Mira suspected poison and considered Rosbet a victim of conspirators who kill heirs.
  • The Baron of Lowville, who owned the Sacred Object, also died of the sea.
  • Small knight Sir Benjamin Womack, meeting the convoy of Harmon, accused the travelers of carrying the mor "from the North Crown", and made everyone undress.
  • Baby G’s mother, who was sheltered by Inge Price, also “takes the mor”. (Inzhi Price)
  • In the Confidential, the abbot's mother explained to the emissary of the church court: when the Subject heals the sysium mor or relieves paralysis, its sacred power is obvious. (The Confidante)

Trivia

  • Mor serves as the measure of every disaster. The rulers of the ducal coffers feared Robert Origin "as the blue sea." News of Adrian's reforms alarmed the Duke of Labelin "worse than the gray sea", and about the horde of Gnoi-gants it was said to be "worse than the gray sea".
  • Mira, bluffing in front of Ayden Almera in June 1774, stated that Leila Talmir had recently died of the blue sea. (Aiden Almera) In fact, Leila was alive.
  • In "Fantasies", the lawyer Mac (by all indications - Mark), guessing that the fisherman Finch would lie for his dog, came up with a dead wife who, dying from the blue sea, allegedly said: "You did not save me, husband. “Save the dog!”
